results.title: Understanding Volvo Auto Tariffs And Their Impact
results.content:
There will be a Volvo tariff effect that reverberates through the entire supply chain. The 25% import tax applies to the entire automotive industry, including car parts and the raw materials used in Volvo production. The price increases will impact not only new automobiles but also pre-owned cars, parts, service prices, and insurance premiums. At the time of writing, the best approach is to buy sooner rather than later.

### How will tariffs affect Volvo parts and servicing? [...] Volvo Cars is working overtime to cushion the impact of the auto tariff on U.S. buyers. While it is too late to stop the immediate influence of these new import taxes, the automaker is hopeful that the market will stabilize once it reduces its dependence on imported products. The company also aims to transfer much of its manufacturing to the United States in the near future to avoid future issues with import tariffs. However, it is still too early to tell the scope of this initiative. [...] Now that the U.S. government's 25% auto tariff has gone into effect, many are wondering – and rightfully so – what this will mean for the automotive industry. Despite having a manufacturing plant in the United States, Volvo prices will inevitably increase over time to cover the cost of foreign-made models and imported auto parts, neither of which are safe from the new tax. results.title: Volvo Group cuts North America forecast by 10K trucks | Trucking Dive
results.content:
### Dive Brief:

### Dive Insight:

Volvo Group faces mounting challenges in one of its largest markets as trade tensions and a freight slowdown cloud its outlook.

In addition to weak demand and supplier pushback, the company will be forced to grapple with a new 25% tariff for imports of heavy-duty and medium-duty trucks and their associated parts beginning Nov. 1. Even before the new levies, the company incurred 500 million SEK in tariff-related costs in Q3 alone, per CFO Mats Backman. [...] Lundstedt said while Volvo Group has a “100% U.S. footprint for North American trucks,” the company is preparing for potential tariff agreements between the U.S. and Mexico.

“We continue to invest and anticipate to have a starting point of around 10,000 units and then with the ability to move north when that is needed,” he said. He further noted that the company has a “structural undercapacity in North America for normal markets and also for upmarkets.” [...] For now, however, it is unlikely Volvo will expand production capacity. The freight recession continues to weigh on demand, and the company expects new tariffs to further slow orders into 2026.

In Q3, Volvo Group’s total truck orders increased by 10% YoY, but deliveries fell by 20% YoY, according to the company’s earnings report. Sales of heavy-duty trucks during the first nine months of 2025 were also down 10% compared to the same period last year.

The country’s exports of larger vehicles have tripled since 2019, with many models containing roughly 50% U.S. content, including diesel engines. New investments, such as Volvo’s planned $700 million factory in Monterrey, highlight the interconnected nature of North American truck production.
